note: Test files that translate no source case. `scripts/parity-check.mjs` requires every collected test to belong to a file that is either a ledger's target file or listed here with a reason, so a whole file of tests cannot sit outside the accounting. A file listed here may not also be a ledger target: a ported file's unmapped tests belong in that ledger's `target_only_tests`, where they are named one by one.

files.why: The canonical encoder's own contract. `tests/test_digest.py` has nothing to say about code-point collation or lone surrogates because in Python both are true by construction -- `sorted()` compares code points and `str.encode('utf-8')` refuses an unpaired surrogate, with no test written for either. Reimplementing those two facts in a language whose defaults are the other way is what created the surface, so the surface gets assertions. The differential oracle checks the same code against real CPython output and is the stronger check; these cases exist so a failure names which property broke.

`project()`'s snapshot guarantee. The Python source has nothing to say about it because there is nothing to say: `Project.aliases` is a `tuple` and cannot be mutated by anyone. In TypeScript `readonly string[]` is a compile-time claim only, so the guarantee has to be made at runtime and asserted -- and it matters because `config_digest` is persisted (DECISIONS.md D-0015).

The differential oracle (docs/porting.md section 4). It makes a claim no ported test can make -- that the artefact CPython produces and the artefact Node produces are the same bytes, on inputs nobody wrote a test about -- so by construction it translates no source case.

The vendored testkit's own contract. `parametrize` is the one piece of machinery the ledger's correctness depends on: if it stopped spelling ids the way pytest does, every mapping in every ledger would still reconcile against the new spelling and nobody would be told.

The composition differential oracle (docs/porting.md section 4.5). The digest oracle questions the encoder; this one questions everything upstream of it -- composition, the layer merge, tombstones and resolution -- by comparing `resolveProject(...).configDigest` against what CPython recorded for the same layer documents. It makes a claim no ported test can make and therefore translates no source case. Measured: a `parseBaseBranch` that NFC-normalises its result leaves all 103 ported tests green, the digest oracle included, and turns this one red on the row named `base-branch-nfd`.

The `os.path` / `pathlib` port's own contract. The Python suite has nothing to say about `posixpath.normpath` or `PureWindowsPath.is_absolute` because in Python they are the standard library; `tests/test_toml_loader.py` asks about them once, and only to explain why `tests/support.py` builds paths as it does. Reimplementing them in a language whose `node:path` answers differently -- on trailing slashes, on two leading slashes, on a `..` inside a UNC anchor -- is what created the surface, and the results reach `LocalPathSource.path` and therefore a persisted digest. Both flavours are asserted on every platform, which a single-platform oracle vector could not do.

The contracts of the other Python built-ins the port had to rebuild: `str.isspace()`, `repr`, `difflib.get_close_matches` and `urlsplit`. Each is a place where the obvious JavaScript spelling gives a different answer -- `/\s/` disagrees with `str.isspace()` in both directions, an edit-distance library is not `SequenceMatcher.ratio`, and `new URL` normalises where `urlsplit` splits -- and what they decide is which catalogs are accepted and what an operator is told when a name is wrong. The Python suite asserts none of it, for the reason `test/domain/canonical-json.test.ts` records: in Python it is all true by construction. The file also carries the frozen-constant cases: `ReadonlySet` is a compile-time claim and `Object.freeze` does nothing to a Set's internal slots, so the `frozenset` the Python side spells had to be rebuilt (DECISIONS.md D-0015). Same reason for being target-only -- the Python suite asserts none of it, because in Python a `frozenset` simply cannot be added to.

G2's capability vocabulary (DECISIONS.md D-0027). There is no Python G2 and none is coming (#25), so this file translates no source case by construction. What it asserts is what an implementation drifts away from silently: that a key is matched by exact equality and never by prefix, that version 1 is exactly the seven keys the entry fixed rather than at least them, that every known version contains its predecessor, and that the frozen set cannot be added to at runtime -- the last because a ReadonlySet is a compile-time claim and Object.freeze does nothing to a Set's internal slots (D-0015), so VOCABULARY_VERSION_1.add(...) would widen every contract pinned at version 1 at an unchanged digest.

The delegation contract's issue-time refusals (docs/design/g2-delegation-contract.md section 5). Target-only for the same reason: no Python G2 exists to have written these cases. Each case is built against one rule's hole and is valid in every other respect, which is the bar cadenza#32 sets -- a refusal is covered only if removing it turns red the case that reproduces that hole, not merely some case somewhere.

contract_digest (docs/design/g2-delegation-contract.md section 6). Target-only: no Python G2. The cases are written as distinctions -- two contracts differing only in one field must not share a digest -- because a digest that quietly ignored grantee or supersedes would let two parties agree on a digest while meaning different contracts, which is the one job it has. It also pins config_digest against a fixed value, so that G2 reusing the sha256 framing shows up here as well as in the CPython oracle if it ever stops being invisible.

The three-valued classifier (docs/design/g2-delegation-contract.md section 7). Target-only: there is no Python G2 and none is coming (#25). Two halves. The first pins one case per row of the section 7 tables, so a failure names the row that moved. The second is the falsifier cadenza#32 asks for -- a deterministic property sweep asserting that no input reaches a fourth state and none throws, seeded with a constant so it cannot become flaky under the double-green rule (D-0006), and required to reach every outcome and every reason so a corpus that degenerated into 20,000 identical refusals would fail rather than pass quietly. It earned its place immediately: it found that sorting the keys for a deterministic reason handed a non-string to a code-point collation, which threw -- a fourth state wearing an exception, on an input no hand-written case had thought to try.

Supersession and onward delegation (docs/design/g2-delegation-contract.md section 8). Target-only: there is no Python G2 and none is coming (#25). The cases are written against what each rule is for rather than against its shape -- "at most one current contract per run" is what makes "under which contract did it do that" answerable, and the subset rule in both directions is what stops a run widening itself by delegating to a helper and reading the answer back. Two of them exist because the mutation check found the rule they cover was uncovered: an askable set reaching past everything the granter holds, and a sub-contract inheriting a lineage that belongs to its granter's grantee.

The agent-type record's issue-time refusals and its immutability (DECISIONS.md D-0031, with the schema fixed by D-0034). Target-only by construction: the record is G2-adjacent, there is no Python G2 and the Python G1 is retired (#25, D-0032), so no case here translates a source case. The refusal cases meet the bar cadenza#32 sets -- each is built against one rule's hole and is valid in every other respect, so removing that rule turns exactly that case red. The immutability cases exist because `readonly` is a compile-time claim and the record carries a digest a run persists: a caller who keeps its input array, its loop policy or its executor policy and mutates one afterwards would otherwise change a record that was already addressed by digest, which is the failure D-0015 records. They are asserted by mutating what the caller still holds and by casting past the `readonly`, because `Object.isFrozen` alone does not show that a write throws.

`agent_type_digest` (D-0031 section 2, D-0034 section 5). Target-only: no Python side, for the reason `test/domain/agent-type.test.ts` records. The cases are written as distinctions -- two records differing only in one field must not share a digest -- because a digest that quietly ignored the model tier would let a host record 'this run used that policy' while the policy it names had changed, which is the one job D-0031 gives it. The executor policy is covered precisely because nothing in cadenza reads it. The file also pins a golden canonical JSON and a golden digest: the payload's snake_case key spellings become a wire format the moment a host persists a digest, and the golden is what makes changing one a failure rather than a silent re-issue of every record in existence. No CPython oracle vector is added, and the reason is not that the oracle covers these shapes -- it does not, being built entirely from `Project` values whose payload holds no number at all. The integer is the one shape this payload adds over `config_digest`, and its spelling is pinned directly by `test/domain/canonical-json.test.ts`, exactly as `contract_digest`'s own `vocabulary_version` already relies on.

The issuance renderer, and the two regression guards D-0031 section 2 asks for. Target-only: no Python side. The renderer's load-bearing case is that what it returns goes into `delegationContract()` and comes out a valid contract, which is what 'the record is inputs to contract construction rather than a second authority' means in code (D-0031 section 1). The guards are here rather than in the domain file because the failure they watch for is invisible from inside the agent-type belt: a record reaching `Project` / `ResolvedProject` would move every project's `config_digest`, every already-issued contract pins the old one, and `classify()`'s first step would return `refused` / `stale_subject` for all of them -- a mass revocation triggered by editing an agent type. So `configDigest` is pinned against a fixed value and `ResolvedProject`'s key set is pinned against its shape.
